Casi todo lo grabado lleva reverberación: Almost everything recorded has added reverberation; without it, a voice sounds “in a box”. Studios use rooms whose reverberation has been measured, and programs imitate it by recording the echo of a gunshot in a real cathedral and applying it to any sound (the impulse response). Sonar and ultrasound are echoes used for measuring: the return time multiplied by the speed of sound, divided by two. And the feedback that howls at a concert is an echo between the microphone and the loudspeaker with $g > 1$: the series that diverges.

En una sala, el sonido no vuelve una vez: In a room, the sound does not come back once: it bounces off every wall, the ceiling, the floor, and reaches the ear by thousands of paths of different lengths, each with its delay and its attenuation. No echo can be distinguished; the sum is a tail of sound that fades away gently, the reverberation. It is measured by the reverberation time $T_{60}$: how long the tail takes to fall 60 decibels, a thousandth of the amplitude. A room has 0.4 s; a concert hall, 2; a cathedral, 8.
It is the geometric series of [[fn-series]]. With $g = 0{.}5$, the sum of all the echoes is twice the original knock; with $g = 0{.}9$, ten times. And with $g \ge 1$ the series diverges: each echo is as loud as or louder than the previous, the room “feeds back” and the sound grows without stopping. The synthesiser clips, but real equipment howls. The convergence condition of a series is the condition for an echo to die away.

No hace falta la exponencial compleja pa: You do not need the complex exponential to understand it: a sine of frequency $k/d$ goes round exactly $k$ times in $d$ seconds, so its delayed copy coincides with it and reinforces it; one of frequency $(k + \frac{1}{2})/d$ arrives half a turn out of phase and subtracts. The spectrum is left with teeth equally spaced every $1/d$ hertz: a comb. With $d = 1$ ms, teeth every 1000 Hz; and since the teeth are at $f, 2f, 3f\ldots$, the comb sounds like a note of frequency $1/d$. It is what Karplus-Strong does in [[son-ruido]]: a very resonant comb.

Si el retardo baja de unas 30 milésimas,: If the delay drops below about 30 thousandths of a second, the ear no longer separates the echo from the original: it fuses them. And what is heard then is a change of timbre, because adding a signal to a delayed copy of itself reinforces some frequencies and cancels others. A sine whose period equals the delay adds in phase with itself: it doubles. One with twice the period arrives inverted: it cancels.
Un [[son-filtros|filtro]] recordaba la m: A [[son-filtros|filter]] remembered the previous sample. An echo remembers what sounded half a second ago and adds it, quieter. And thousands of tiny, disordered echoes are the reverberation of a room: the sound of the space.

Wallace Sabine, un físico joven de Harva: Wallace Sabine, a young Harvard physicist, was asked in 1895 to fix the acoustics of a lecture hall where nothing could be understood. He spent two years measuring with an organ pipe and a stopwatch how long a note took to die away while he moved cushions about, and discovered that the time was proportional to the volume and inversely proportional to the absorption. With that formula he designed Boston's Symphony Hall (1900), still one of the best halls in the world, and founded architectural acoustics. Artificial reverberation arrived in the 1950s with steel plates and springs, and in 1961 Manfred Schroeder published how to do it with delays and gains in a computer: essentially, the third synthesiser above.
